articles.title: 'I'd talk to the TV': The paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonely
articles.summary: As loneliness grows in China, a new industry is emerging to provide companionship and support.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: Why the lonely in China are hiring 'temporary children' By Stephen McDonell 
China correspondent 
- Published 2 hours ago 
"The biggest difficulty really was the loneliness. Sometimes, if I wanted to talk to someone I'd talk to the TV." 
Yang, 91, lives on the outskirts of China's bustling capital Beijing. Following the death of her husband, she was so lonely that she says she even considered the possibility of voluntary euthanasia. 
"I asked my son about it but he told me it was banned. I told him that if it ever becomes legal I want to do it - I didn't want to live any longer." 
Suffering glaucoma, with failing eyesight, she was unable to even do basic things like adjust the controls on her air conditioner. 
Cases such as Yang's have become increasingly common in Chinese cities which Associate Professor Teresa Kuan, from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, says is "exacerbated by the structure of society and the modes by which people interact". 
There are many causes of isolation in China. Like when rural migrants pursue economic opportunities, leaving behind close-knit support networks for urban centres where loneliness and uncertainty can be difficult to overcome, or when graduates uproot themselves chasing employment on the other side of the country. 
Image caption, 
Suffering from glaucoma and failing eyesight, 91-year-old Yang found simple tasks and daily life increasingly difficult on her own. 
But now a growing "loneliness industry" has emerged to try to fill these gaps in people's lives. 
Yang says her life has been transformed by one of these services - Wang Yingwei and his electric scooter delivery team - who started coming over twice a day with hot meals but whose help extends far beyond that. 
"We see ourselves as community children," Yingwei told the BBC. "It means putting yourself in the shoes of older people and carefully considering their needs. 
"For example, they may be drinking tap water which can be cloudy and contain a lot of lime. I can fix this problem with a filtered water tank. Such a small thing can make them much happier. Maybe they can't shower because their equipment is broken. I'll buy a part, replace it and their shower is fine." 
"The elderly treat us like their children, and we treat them like our own parents," he added. 
Yingwei's services cost less than half the price of employing a caregiver. 
Image caption, 
Wang Yingwei and his small delivery team offer more than just meals, bringing human connection to elderly residents. 
The former mobile phone salesman says he started his company to help seniors remain at home without having to move into retirement facilities. He was inspired to do this after his own father-in-law, who had developed Alzheimer's, had to go into a nursing home. Yingwei said he felt that the conditions there were so sub-standard he wanted to make sure others could stay out of institutions like this for as long as possible. 
His small business currently employs four people but he says there is a possibility he will expand as demand grows. 
There is still a shortage of solid data on the size of this sector – which operators say has exploded in recent years – but securities company Sinolink valued it at around $7.4 billion in 2025. And this is only expected to grow given the trajectory of modern lifestyles. 
Zheng Ruizhi, another client of Yingwei's who lives in Beijing's northern outskirts, welcomed him at the door with a big smile. 
"After retiring, I don't have much opportunity to hang out with others," the 75-year-old, whose son lives two hours away from her, told the BBC. 
She was recovering from a recent injury which she said was making everyday tasks more difficult. 
Image caption, 
Zheng Ruizhi, 75, shares a lighthearted moment with Wang Yingwei during a home visit. 
But the arrival of Yingwei – who she calls her "dear boy" – lightened her mood. 
"I call you 'dear boy' because I am so fond of you. I genuinely like you from the bottom of my heart. I also admire and trust you. When you help me out, I don't have a single worry or fear," she told him. 
Yet the services offered by those in this sector are not limited to home visits. 
Twenty-three-year-old Liu Yanyan, for instance, works as a "medical escort". She acts as a friendly face taking clients to see the doctor, or picking up their test results or medication from city hospitals, which can be intimidatingly large and bureaucratic. 
"Some of my customers are people in their 20s who came to Beijing to build a career. They might not have friends here or feel awkward asking colleagues to accompany them because of the concept of social reciprocity in Chinese culture," she said. "If I accompanied you to a doctor's appointment for free, you might feel obligated to buy me a meal or a movie ticket afterwards." 
She said that, because of this, there are many people in modern Chinese society who tend to keep to themselves. 
"So, they hire someone like me to accompany them to the hospital. If they had to go alone, they could feel scared or anxious." 
Image caption, 
Liu Yanyan, a 23-year-old medical escort, helps clients navigate complex city hospitals. 
At the core of many businesses catering to loneliness in China is a simple offering: human connection. 
Teresa Kuan said that some people prefer the option of pouring their hearts out to a complete stranger for a fee. 
"If there is a companion you have paid for, the relationship is not exactly equal. It is a service relationship, so you don't have to deal with the unpredictability of a standard relationship. The thing about friendship is that it can be unpredictable. You don't know when someone might disappoint you. But, in a service relationship, you have a better idea of what to expect." 
Wang Zhoutao runs a hiking business to help people who want to climb China's famous mountain Huangshan in Anhui Province. 
"We provide emotional support, like cheering them up, taking their photo or telling jokes. It's really a service based on companionship," he said. 
The former soldier added that he normally hikes up the mountain with clients 10 to 15 days a month. When fully booked, this could be as many as 30 times a month. 
Image caption, 
Mountain escort Wang Zhoutao guides a client up the steep steps of Mount Huangshan. 
He gave an example of a young woman he once accompanied who felt ostracised at work. "She felt useless and wanted to prove something to herself," he said. 
"We started climbing but it was a tough trek as the weather was really hot and we were sweating a lot. There were moments she wanted to give up but I told her, 'If you quit now and can't get over this mountain how will you handle anything else in life?'. I kept encouraging her." 
After they made it all the way he said she sent him a long message of thanks describing her inner journey and expressing her gratitude. 
"The pace of life is just too fast these days. People face pressure from work, relationships and family expectations," he said. "I think my clients are mostly people who feel a void in their relationships or have suffered a setback." 
Human connection is a necessity but, in a society grappling with loneliness across generations, it has now also become a commodity. 
Back in her little Beijing flat, Yang is feeling more comfortable now that Yingwei has sorted out her problem of making the air conditioner work properly. 
"It's good to have someone around when you need it, someone you can share your innermost thoughts with," she said. 
"I did struggle with loneliness but that's been resolved now. I'm quite happy. 
"I can't lose Yingwei and the others. They've all got a good heart."

articles.title: The island where locals say data centres are taking their water
articles.summary: "Not a single drop has come through our taps for the last three months," a local tells the BBC.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Batam's reservoirs are under pressure as the island aims to be a digital hub By Muhammad Islahuddin ,  Reporting from Batam   and   Kelly Ng ,  Reporting from Singapore 
- Published 12 October 2026 
"Water! Water!" the crowd shouted as it stormed a compound with data centres, armed with empty plastic bottles and jerry cans. 
There were about 300 of them, all residents on the Indonesian island of Batam, and they were furious that the taps at home had run dry, while the data centres in the new Nongsa Digital Park seemed to have enough water to protect their machines from overheating. 
"Not a single drop has come through our taps for the last three months... Our water supply had been reliable until the data centres came," Dewi Susanti, one of the protesters, told the BBC. 
People in her village, Bakau Serip, were now depending on tanker trucks that dispensed "dirty, cloudy and smelly" water, she said. 
Batam's water utility told the BBC it was working to improve supply, but did not comment on whether the disruption was linked to demand from the data centres. 
But BP Batam, the agency overseeing trade and industry, blamed it on a prolonged dry spell and denied allegations from locals that water meant for homes was being channelled to data centres. 
This is not the first such protest in Batam, whose shrinking reservoirs find themselves under more pressure as the island tries to transform itself into a digital hub. 
Following protests in August and September, authorities told the firms opening data centres in Batam that they must build their own desalination plants instead of relying on reservoirs for freshwater. 
But locals say they are increasingly concerned that they must now compete with servers for water. 
"Reliable data on data centre water use in Indonesia remains scarce, partly because companies treat it as proprietary information," says Agus Hasan, a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology. 
"We should build [data centres] rationally, transparently, and responsibly, and insist on seeing the numbers... [Otherwise] those kept in the dark while their taps run dry will push back, and rightly so," he adds. 
Image caption, 
Batam residents protesting over water shortage 
A backlash has been building against data centres across the world, from the US to the UK to parts of Asia, as tech companies pour billions into AI infrastructure. 
People are worried about how the huge, windowless buildings might change their neighbourhoods, the constant hum of machines, the security lights that could stay on all night, and the pressure this puts on water and energy resources. 
While electricity powers the centres, the water keeps the servers from frying – engineers deploy elaborate cooling systems, which consume a lot of water. 
Research in the US suggests a typical data centre consumes around 300,000 gallons of water a day, or about as much as 1,000 US households. A larger, 50MW facility could take as much water as 2,200 households per day, and enough electricity to power 22,000 homes, according to Malaysia's central bank. 
It's unclear how much water or electricity the data centres in Batam are consuming. 
But the island routinely faces water shortages, and the levels are worse this year, possibly because of a historic "super" El Niño. 
Devoid of natural freshwater sources, Batam's 1.3 million people rely on rainwater collected in six artificial reservoirs. 
Nongsa reservoir, which supplies water to Bakau Serip, where Dewi lives, would dry up over the next month with no rainfall, simulations by local environmental non-profit group Akar Bhumi Indonesia suggest. 
"The water shortage is affecting our livelihoods... Money that should be used to buy rice is now spent on water drums," Dewi says. "My husband has to wait up overnight to get water, and then go straight to work the next morning." 
Batam's water utility had earlier said that it would consider measures like cloud seeding should the water shortage continue. When asked about the recent protests, they pointed us to earlier statements. 
Image source, BBC/ Muhammad Islahuddin Image caption, 
A view of the data centres inside Batam's Nongsa Digital Park 
Authorities in Batam have approved 10 data centres, six of which will be located in Nongsa Digital Park. Two are up and running, while a third is under construction. At least six more are currently under review for approval, BP Batam told the BBC. 
Official figures put investment in data centres on the island at more than $6.7bn (£5.1bn) as of mid-2026, spurred in part by demand from Singapore, which is just an hour away by ferry. 
Singapore paused construction of data centres in 2019, citing land and energy constraints. It lifted the ban in 2022 after introducing new efficiency standards, which prompted investors to look elsewhere. 
Singapore has long been promoting the Riau Islands, which includes Batam, and the Malaysian state of Johor as "complementary" regions. 
Quick to absorb the spillover, Johor approved data centre projects worth tens of billions. But this soon drew the ire of residents frustrated with noise, dust and water shortages. The state has since tried to regulate how much water and electricity data centres consume. 
Across the strait, Batam is just as attractive to investors – from the US, China, Australia, Singapore – because of relatively low operating costs, proximity to Singapore and connections to major subsea cable routes. 
Image source, BBC/ Muhammad Islahuddin Image caption, 
A data centre under construction in Nongsa 
Nongsa is home to a 13,000-sq-m data centre by Hong Kong-based private equity firm Gaw Capital and Indonesian developer Sinar Primera. In April, Singapore's DayOne signed a deal with an Indonesian state utility to build one of the country's largest data centres with around 450MW capacity, enough to power 350,000 average households. In June, DayOne, chip maker Nvidia and Australian AI start-up Firmus Technologies announced a 360MW "AI factory". 
By 2030, power demand from data centres in Batam is expected to cross 1,100MW, which is enough to power nearly a million homes, according to the official estimates. 
The BBC has contacted DayOne, Sinar Primera and Gaw Capital for comment. 
Meanwhile, the spate of construction is worrying locals in Batam who urged authorities to prioritise their needs. 
"Don't just sit at the top and keep approving these projects. Come down here and see for yourselves what we are wrestling with," says Marlinda, who lives in the district of Sei Beduk, which is also facing water shortages. 
"We want the government to pay attention to ordinary people," another resident told the BBC. 
"Don't make billion-rupiah investments while ordinary people are made to suffer... We are not asking for anything extravagant. We just want our water supply restored."

articles.title: Homes and bridges swept away as fresh floods hit Nepal
articles.summary: Nepal is still trying to recover from catastrophic floods that hit less than two months ago, leaving thousands dead and missing.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Flash flood washes building complex in central Nepal By Navin Singh Khadka Environment correspondent, BBC World Service 
- Published 11 October 2026 Updated 12 October 2026 
A major river in Nepal has flooded, sweeping away houses, bridges and damaging a part of hydropower station, authorities have said. 
Officials say they have rescued 95 people, including nine foreigners, along the bank of the Budhi Gandaki River in the central Gorkha district, the army confirmed. No casualties have been reported yet, however five people are missing. 
A video of the flood shows the moment raging waters sweep down a valley and wash away an entire building complex. 
Nepal is on high alert and still trying to recover from catastrophic floods that hit its border towns with Tibet two months ago, leaving more than 1,400 people dead and thousands missing. 
Sunday's flood tore through the Gorkha district as children and communities prepared to mark the first day of the Dashain festival, a major moment in the Nepali calendar. 
More than 200 homes were damaged and more than 650 people were impacted by the flood, Nepal's Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said. 
Some settlements have been completely cut off and are now only accessible by air, a local official told The Kathmandu Post. 
Nepal's army said it had mobilised four helicopters for search and rescue operations. 
Families have been forced to flee their homes, with many facing uncertainty over where they will find safe shelter and access to essential supplies. 
Ganesh Karki, a resident of Jagatbagar, told The Kathmandu Post that he and others took shelter about 500m (0.3 miles) uphill in a nearby forest after receiving a warning call about the flood early in the morning. 
"We never imagined a flood of this size," he said. "The water surged for about 15 minutes and then stopped repeatedly throughout the morning. We are afraid to return home at night." 
The flood swept away about a dozen houses and several suspension bridges, while a hydroelectric project was damaged, carrying some of the construction equipment away, the disaster management authority said. 
Within a couple of hours, the river's water levels at one location had risen from two metres (6ft 5in) to nearly 8.5m (27ft 9in), officials said. 
Binod Parajuli, a meteorologist who works with the Nepalese government, said: "Our hydrological station was swept away and we are not getting any data from that location." 
However, experts say the debris-flow is much smaller and travelled more slowly than the devastating flash floods in August. 
What caused the latest flood is still unclear. Some say a landslide may have blocked the river or its tributary for some time, causing the dammed water to burst out, while others say locals upstream saw an ice-avalanche. 
Save the Children is mobilising an emergency team to respond to Sunday's flood. 
"Children's lives have been ripped apart in an instant yet again", the charity's director in Nepal, Tara Chettry, said. 
"We are yet to see the full scale of the damage, but they may have lost their homes, schools and communities. Many children in Gorkha will still be in shock and distress after the mega floods in August, barely having a chance to get back on their feet." 
The Budhi Gandaki is a tributary of the Trishuli river, downstream from another tributary where an avalanche of rock and ice in August caused floods along the Nepal-Tibet border. The avalanche happened near the peak of Lantang Lirung, a mountain on Nepal's side of the Himalayas. Hundreds of people were killed in those floods. 
Nepal is prone to disasters, from earthquakes to landslides and floods, as a result of the unpredictable natural environment in the Himalayas. 
Experts say climate change, which is making glaciers melt faster, is likely raising the risk of such disasters, leaving local communities increasingly vulnerable.

articles.title: MI5 chief warns of threats to UK from Russia, Iran and AI
articles.summary: Sir Ken McCallum says operations to tackle terrorism and state threats are now roughly of an "equal scale".
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: State threats and AI - Key takeaways from MI5 chief's speech By Frank Gardner ,  Security correspondent ,  Reporting from Thames House   and   Adam Goldsmith 
- Published 13 October 2026 
MI5 is devoting more resource to countering state threats than during the Cold War, the head of the intelligence service has said. 
Sir Ken McCallum said threats from foreign adversaries had quadrupled in the last decade, with Russia "aggressor number one" as well as increased Iran-linked aggression against Jewish sites and military bases. 
At an annual speech in London, MI5's chief said Russia was waging hybrid warfare at a time when AI was "supercharging the cyber-security contest between attackers and defenders". 
He also warned of rising threats from "extreme right-wing terrorism" and said MI5 had "caught terrorists seeking to exploit AI," including by integrating the technology with drones. 
He said the biggest threat from the misuse of AI was extremist groups using the technology to harness new and existing bioweapons. 
However, he noted that work countering terrorism and state threats was now "pretty much of equal scale" which he described as a "huge shift" in recent years. 
Sir Ken said Russia had stopped short of "conventional conflict" against Nato and is instead trying to unsettle European countries while its progress in its full-scale invasion of Ukraine is "minimal and horrifically costly". 
Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyber-attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary. 
These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary. 
Sir Ken said MI5 successes in identifying and expelling Russian spies from the UK had left the Kremlin dependent on paying proxies for attempted attacks. 
"With its traditional covert footprint eviscerated by almost 1,000 expulsions since the invasion, the Kremlin's global toolkit is weak, he said. 
"So we see them scrambling to pay criminals to do their bidding." 
He added: "These are not the actions of a great power with the strategic upper hand." 
His comments come as a growing number of leaders across Europe have warned Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine. 
Asked after the speech about Prime Minister Andy Burnham's recent comments that Russia interfered with the Brexit referendum , Sir Ken said it was "not new news" that there had been attempts from Moscow but distinguished between "interference attempted" and "outcome achieved". 
He said it was a matter of public record that there were pieces in Russian media and "so-called internet trolls and bot farms" seeking to influence the Brexit debate, but also stressed that the result of the 2016 referendum was "not in dispute". 
He added that he was "worried" about the the ongoing debate on Russian interference. 
"I am a little bit anxious that we don't play into our adversaries' hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall," he told reporters. 
Image source, PA Media Image caption, 
Sir Ken McCallum gave his annual address at MI5's headquarters in central London 
Meanwhile, Sir Ken warned that Iran is also expanding a hybrid campaign in the UK. 
The intelligence chief said there had been 50 arrests in the last year over Iran-linked activities. 
Much of this Iranian aggression has been aimed at Jewish communities, Sir Ken added, and also at "harder targets, like military sites". 
Sir Ken did not mention arrests at RAF Fairford directly during his speech, but told reporters afterwards the incident was "not unique". 
He added: "We have seen Iranian interest beyond RAF Fairford in the UK." 
The incident at the airbase in Gloucesteshire, where three suspicious vans were seen parked nearby, has seen seven people arrested and bailed by counter-terrorism police. 
Burnham has said the incident was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard". 
The MI5 head said in his speech: "What I can say is that those who seek to cause mayhem on British streets - whether hired thugs here or their paymasters overseas - will meet an unflinching response." 
Sir Ken added that the National Security Act - a 2023 law designed to target people working against UK interests for foreign powers - is in heavy use, and has been employed to tackle threats from China as well as Iran and Russia. 
On the emerging threat posed by AI, Sir Ken said: "It can produce propaganda and radicalising material tailored to the individual. 
"We've caught terrorists seeking to exploit Al to improve their reconnaissance and attack methodologies, with Al-enabled drones adding a new twist." 
Sir Ken said the bioweapons threat posed by AI was "not yet realised" but warned the technology has the "potential to change the stakes". 
"These risks are real. The UK Intelligence Community - MI5, GCHQ, MI6 - is working closely with the UK's globally respected AI Security Institute to take them on." 
Sir Ken said AI poses unknown threats, telling Thames House: "Put at its simplest, human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are". 
He announced MI5 had launched an AI Threat Assessment Centre, which he said would assess sources and "separate the bluster from the realities". 
In April, the UK's terrorism threat level was raised to severe for the first time in five years, meaning an attack is highly likely. 
Sir Ken said Islamist groups like Al Qaeda and so-called Islamic State both continue to direct and inspire attacks, while the increased risk was also driven "in significant part" by extreme right-wing terrorism. 
He continued: "Over the last year the most marked trend has been an increase in cases where extremist versions of anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievance are tipping into terrorist intent." 
Sir Ken said extreme right-wing terrorism tended to "skew young", driven by the internet - adding that MI5 had in recent months investigated a "radicalised extreme right-wing 13-year-old here in the UK". 
He said: "That investigation generated insight that enabled one of our international partners to prevent a lethal attack on their soil."

Graduate student accused of poisoning colleague and trying to flee to China arrested at LAX
Microbiologist Aili Wang, 32, poisoned tea of colleague in Wyoming who had pending patents, prosecutors allege 
A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents and with whom she did not get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her. 
Aili Wang, 32, was arrested 6 October at Los Angeles international airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China . With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in technology for disease treatment – research similar to work she had done in China. 
Wang remained jailed without bail Tuesday in Los Angeles. She allegedly bought a chemical, acrylamide, over eBay, and it was first detected when the alleged victim’s wife and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea. 
US officials for years have accused China of stealing intellectual property from American universities. 
The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations left him reeling. He was uncertain if the victim will fully recover. 
“It’s been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your students’ lives is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that,” Gomelsky told the Associated Press. “That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career.” 
Wang had no attorney listed in court documents. The AP tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages. 
The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as “KT”, began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical in the coffee maker water. The victim and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie. 
Wang allegedly was recorded 27 September going through the alleged victim’s desk. On 1 October, she was recorded “taking photos and manipulating notebooks” on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer’s affidavit said. 
Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit. 
The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a prestigious conference in August, Gomelsky said. 
He also noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said. When he washed the coffee maker, Gomelsky said, the taste would go away. 
Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the graduate student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide. 
Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine. 
It’s not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany county circuit court judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors’ request and raised bond to $1.5m cash-only. 
Wang allegedly asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer, police said.

articles.title: It’s My Time review – Michelle Yeoh excels in Rocky-style quest to be Rubik’s Cube champ
articles.summary: True story about a former maths teacher who became a puzzle champion in retirement is squeezed into predictable sports-movie formulaIt’s not quite up there with Leonardo DiCaprio eating raw bison liver to get into character, but Michelle Yeoh reportedly spent two years learning the Rubik’s Cube to prepare for this Chinese drama in which she plays a real-life former maths teacher who became a champion in retirement. The true story is stretched and squeezed here, fictionalised to fit sports-movie formula; it ends up being so-so entertaining and funny in places, but disappointingly predictable. The biggest surprise is that cubing is so popular it has its own world championship.Still, Yeoh gives a superb, spiky performance as blunt, foul-tempered Zhao Yanhong; following a stroke, Zhao is living in a nursing home where she is the resident badass, assaulting her robot care companion and making illicit trips to the off-licence. She discovers her natural talent for the Rubik’s Cube when a washed-up ex-champion called Wu Youwei (Haoran Liu) comes to the nursing home to give a tutorial. What follows is a classic sports-film structure, with qualifying heats and Zhao training day and night, lifting weights and pounding the city streets. (Yes, running is de rigueur in a Rubik’s Cube movie; physical strength is Zhao’s weak spot says Wu, who agrees to be her coach.) Continue reading...

It’s My Time review – Michelle Yeoh excels in Rocky-style quest to be Rubik’s Cube champ
True story about a former maths teacher who became a puzzle champion in retirement is squeezed into predictable sports-movie formula 
I t’s not quite up there with Leonardo DiCaprio eating raw bison liver to get into character, but Michelle Yeoh reportedly spent two years learning the Rubik’s Cube to prepare for this Chinese drama in which she plays a real-life former maths teacher who became a champion in retirement. The true story is stretched and squeezed here, fictionalised to fit sports-movie formula; it ends up being so-so entertaining and funny in places, but disappointingly predictable. The biggest surprise is that cubing is so popular it has its own world championship. 
Still, Yeoh gives a superb, spiky performance as blunt, foul-tempered Zhao Yanhong; following a stroke, Zhao is living in a nursing home where she is the resident badass, assaulting her robot care companion and making illicit trips to the off-licence. She discovers her natural talent for the Rubik’s Cube when a washed-up ex-champion called Wu Youwei (Haoran Liu) comes to the nursing home to give a tutorial. What follows is a classic sports-film structure, with qualifying heats and Zhao training day and night, lifting weights and pounding the city streets. (Yes, running is de rigueur in a Rubik’s Cube movie; physical strength is Zhao’s weak spot says Wu, who agrees to be her coach.) 
Yeoh is enjoyably irascible as Zhao, who goes viral after thrashing a kid in her first competition. Her online fans call her “Grandma Zhao” and the film gently chips away at stereotypes of the older generation; fans assume Zhao is a cuddly elder, while younger cubers underestimate her skill and stamina. Yeoh brings intelligence to the role, but it’s odd that after making Zhao so testy and short-tempered, the film is all soft edges with a squishy centre. Next, can we expect a biopic of the six-year-old Chinese girl who recently set a Rubik’s Cube world record , solving it in just over four seconds?

‘Super app’ aimed at UK students uses servers owned by Chinese firm on US blacklist
ZyMix platform has contract with Tencent, which US alleges has links to People’s Liberation Army 
A new messaging and payment “super app” marketed at British students uses servers owned by a Chinese company that has been put on a US military blacklist for its alleged affiliation to the People’s Liberation Army. 
ZyMix, which is being pushed on university campuses as the UK’s first super app designed “for gen Z”, combining chat, payments and community features, has a contract with a German-based subsidiary of Tencent Holdings, a Chinese conglomerate in Shenzhen. 
Tencent Holdings was added in January 2026 to the US Department of Defense’s (DoD) list of Chinese military companies, which is formally known as the section 1260H list. 
The citation on the DoD list says that the company, which is a gaming and social media conglomerate, is indirectly affiliated to the Chinese People’s Liberation Army. 
The blacklist is part of a US attempt to counteract what it regards as Beijing’s efforts to increase its military power by using technology from Chinese firms, universities and research programmes. 
The DoD is prohibited from entering into, renewing or extending contracts for goods, services or technology with any entity on the list although wider sanctions are not automatic. 
A Tencent spokesperson said: “Tencent’s inclusion on this list is clearly a mistake. We are not a military company or supplier. Unlike sanctions or export controls, this listing has no impact on our business. We will nonetheless work with the Department of Defense to address any misunderstanding.” 
China’s footprint in higher education in the UK has become a controversial issue. MI5 recently warned British universities to cut ties with the China General Technology Research Institute. MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities 
Read more 
The domestic intelligence service claimed it was secretly channelling funding from Beijing’s intelligence apparatus to UK-linked academics to improve the technical espionage capabilities of China’s ministry of state security. 
The link between the Chinese-owned infrastructure and ZyMix was initially disclosed in the company’s privacy policy at the time of its launch last week. 
The document, which is legally required, said that Tencent (Frankfurt) stored user-generated content and messages. After the Guardian approached the company, the privacy policy was rewritten and mention of Tencent was removed. 
The policy now states that users’ personal data is stored and processed primarily in the United Kingdom and the EU, adding that “some of our service providers are located in other countries, including the United States”. 
It goes on to say that “auxiliary infrastructure providers, hosted in the EU, receive only encrypted user messages and limited technical data, such as technical statistics, licence validation when the app starts”. 
A spokesperson said: “As a newly launched startup, we are updating our privacy notice as we develop our services, including clarifying that Tencent, Twilio and the other providers concerned are used solely for performance testing.” 
The spokesperson added: “Our agreement is with Tencent Cloud Europe BV, which we use for auxiliary services, rather than as the provider that stores ZyMix user data. We take our obligations under UK data protection law seriously.” 
The new privacy policy invites those who wish to know the identity of their suppliers to request the information from the company. 
In response to a request from the Guardian, Tarique Ghaffur, a former assistant commissioner at the Metropolitan police, who described himself as a security consultant for ZyMix, responded. 
He said: “We have reviewed your request as against our private privacy [sic] you mentioned. Unfortunately, at the present time for reasons of commercial confidentiality, contractual obligations and legal privileges, we are not able to provide you with the requested information.” 
Fraser Sampson, a professor of security and national governance and formerly the UK’s biometrics and surveillance camera commissioner, said he was “sceptical when ‘commercial confidentiality’ arguments are used to duck basic policy questions and amending policy on the fly is never reassuring”. 
He added: “When companies ask us for our personal data, they should expect us to ask them where it’s being kept, for what purpose(s) and who they’re going to share it with – and be prepared to answer fully.” 
Sam Dunning, the director of the UK-China Transparency NGO, said: “There are serious questions about whether ZyMix have taken due care before launching this product.” 
A spokesperson for ZyMix said: “Whilst still in its beta stage, the ZyMix app has been developed to fully comply with all UK data, privacy and financial regulations.” 
ZyMix is heavily targeting the university market and is offering £200 to £400 a month to people who agree to be brand ambassadors on campuses. Staff roles have also been advertised in the UK by ZyMix for Mandarin-speaking applicants. 
One advert on LinkedIn for the job of operations manager (Mandarin speaking) required “excellent written and verbal communication skills in both English and Mandarin (required for daily communication with the China team)”. 
Separately, a distinct company appeared to be recruiting on behalf of ZyMix on WeChat, the Chinese instant messaging service, saying: “The product, R&D, design and testing team is in Greater China, with branch-company bases covering: Taipei / Shenzhen / Guangzhou / Hangzhou / Chengdu / Zhengzhou.” 
Ghaffur said that Flicknmix, the UK company that publishes the ZyMix app, “does not have any subsidiaries or branch offices in China. Our aim is to create opportunities within the UK”. A spokesperson for ZyMix described it as “British born”.

Stellantis and Renault back UK to get EU car industry protection
Bosses of Citroën owner and French carmaker also urge UK government to consider limiting imports from China 
Stellantis and Renault have backed the UK car industry for inclusion in proposed rules to protect EU industry, but urged the British government to consider limiting imports of Chinese cars. 
Emanuele Cappellano, who leads Stellantis’s European brands including Fiat, Citroën, Opel and Vauxhall, and François Provost, the chief executive of France’s Renault, said the UK should effectively be counted as one of the EU’s 27 member states for the purposes of the proposed “Made in Europe” legislation . 
The new rules aim to ensure EU subsidies and government procurement benefits Europe’s industry, rather than helping manufacturers from other countries. EU to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle imports to 350,000 a year 
Read more 
The executives were speaking at the Paris motor show, which was attended on Monday by the French president, Emmanuel Macron. Brands including Li Auto, GAC and Chery were among a host of Chinese manufacturers exhibiting in Paris with ambitious European expansion plans. 
Europe’s car industry is under enormous pressure as it copes with lower demand than before the coronavirus pandemic, while also investing tens of billions of euros in shifting production to electric vehicles (EVs). At the same time, Chinese carmakers’ market share has soared as the transition to EVs opens the door to new entrants. 
The EU confirmed on Monday it would limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year. The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week. 
The Made in Europe rules are another plank of the EU’s response to the rise of China in key manufacturing industries such as carmaking and chemicals. 
Under the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), cars will have to be “made in Europe”, and contain enough European parts and materials, to continue to qualify for EV grants and to be bought by public bodies in the EU. However, automotive manufacturers and politicians are haggling over the details. 
If Brussels sticks to a strict definition of “European” as being only EU countries, Britain risks being left out – prompting intense lobbying from UK car industry and government to be included. 
Stellantis is among the manufacturers that still has a British factory, its facility in Ellesmere Port, Merseyside, which produces small vans. 
“I think that UK somehow needs to be equalised to the EU 27,” said Cappellano, referring to the bloc’s 27 member states. “We have a lot of relationship, we have footprint. Historically UK has been very close to the European market.” 
Europe’s main automotive lobby groups ACEA and Clepa have also put their weight behind the UK to be included. Some parts of European manufacturing, including France’s industry minister , had argued that the UK should be left out given Brexit. 
Provost said there was “no other choice” but a deal between the UK and EU. However, he said the UK would also have to stop allowing Chinese cars in without limits. 
“On your side, you have also to take decisions,” he said. “If the UK is willing to join the European ecosystem, this is to have an industrial ambition … to keep a strong automotive industry.” skip past newsletter promotion

He said this would be an industry that “is not closed to Chinese competitors, but … if you want to operate in Europe, you have to deeply invest in the whole value chain, final manufacturing, suppliers, R&D, technologies.” 
Provost added: “I’m not here to demand whatsoever, but I think if UK is willing to join this ecosystem of IAA, there is some open question about the level of imports.” 
London has so far rejected pressure to impose its own tariffs on Chinese imports, but the UK business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, this month said that decision was under review . 
Cappellano also said the UK should consider imposing tariffs on Chinese imports. “It’s very important that the UK defines what is the priority,” he said. “It’s very difficult to defend industrial footprint and at the same time let the market completely open to import. Either one or the other.” 
He expressed scepticism over whether other countries beyond the EU such as Japan, Turkey and Morocco should be included in the rules. 
“We don’t necessarily need to have a larger definition of European scope,” he said, pointing to proposals that carmakers be allowed to source 30% of their materials from outside the EU. 
He also argued for more time until 2030 for manufacturers to source batteries from within Europe. China is dominant in the global supply of batteries and Cappellano said it would take longer to build up the European industry.

The EU is to limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year, the European Commission has confirmed. 
Imports have been soaring in the past two years; about 800,000 battery and plug-in hybrids are likely to be sold this year. 
The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week . 
The annual limit on imports of hybrids will be taken under the World Trade Organization safeguard measures, which mean it can be implemented swiftly without the type of investigations needed in anti-dumping measures. Read more 
Any cars imported above the quota level will not be subject to tariffs, but will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe. 
Chinese vehicles assembled within the EU, such as those made in Hungary or, in future, Spain, will not be subject to the quota, officials have confirmed, but EU companies making cars in China will. 
China’s exports of hybrids to the EU tripled to €6.7bn (£5.7bn) in the first half of this year, from €2.2bn a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data. 
As part of the deal, China has also agreed to drop some tariffs on auto parts and cut duties by half on footwear, olive oil and ice-cream from the EU. 
Officials stressed that the quota is fully supported by China, and further dialogue on cars and other imports including chemicals, renewable energy and furniture is continuing. 
“We will continue the dialogue on some products … this is by no means the end of the story,” an official said. 
Last month, the EU called for feedback on a new rule that could oblige companies to diversify their supply chains while the “Made in Europe” legislation would do the same in public procurement. 
On Thursday, EU leaders will discuss a French-German proposal for a “kill switch” or new instrument that would allow Brussels to block access to the single market for certain goods in the event of any harmful development, such as a ban on rare earths crucial for the tech and automotive industries. skip past newsletter promotion

The deal on hybrid EVs comes amid mounting concern over the £1bn-a-day trade deficit the EU is now running with China. 
Up until recently, the EU’s strategy for tackling what it says is an “unsustainable” trade imbalance has been to seek to increase exports to China. 
Sources said there has been “a paradigm shift” with concerns of deindustrialisation and job losses in the industrial heartlands forcing a renewed focus on curbing imports rather than increasing exports. 
“We are closely surveilling, our imports. We know what’s coming in. We know where there’s a surge, and we know what hits the hardest in terms of our deindustrialisation,” said an official. 
Andrew Small, the director of the Asia programme at the European Council for Foreign Relations, said China was likely to “suck the EU into drawn-out negotiations” on other sectors but the mood had changed in the EU. 
“I think if China had offered a deal like this earlier in the year, say in spring, it would have been much easier to take the heat out. My sense is that things have now moved somewhat too far politically,” he said.

Volkswagen boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic European industry
Oliver Blume says ‘Made in Europe’ rules to counter rapid rise of lower-price Chinese brands ‘must reward real value creation’ 
The boss of Volkswagen has backed EU proposals to boost its domestic industry, arguing European carmakers need to be able to “compete under comparable conditions” with Chinese rivals. 
Oliver Blume said “Made in Europe” rules from the EU “must reward real value creation in Europe”, speaking in Paris before the motor show this week. 
The rules are aimed at countering the rapid rise of Chinese brands in Europe in the automotive sector and other important manufacturing industries. Lower-priced Chinese manufacturers have prompted a crisis in several industries. 
Volkswagen is among the most-affected European companies. Germany’s biggest carmaker has launched a brutal plan to cut as many as 100,000 jobs . Blume said it was the “largest transformation programme in its history”. Alarm bells sound in Brussels as EU sales of Chinese hybrid cars rocket 
Read more 
The proposals for the Made in Europe rules, formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act, would limit subsidies and public procurement to products with a large proportion of their materials and manufacturing coming from within the EU. 
Blume listed a litany of challenges facing European carmakers, saying: “Europe is under enormous competitive pressure.” These included: high energy costs; lower demand as consumers struggle with high inflation; the need to be quicker to develop cars; and intense competition from China . 
On Friday, the EU said it had reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry. 
Blume said Germany’s carmakers were happy to compete with Chinese rivals, but said the EU should try to reward businesses with significant European footprints. 
“Companies that invest and develop in Europe must see a clear benefit,” he said. 
Referring to Chinese companies, he added: “Those who sell here should compete under comparable conditions and create jobs and value here in Europe, too. skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion 
View image in fullscreen 
The new all-electric ID Tiguan. Photograph: Volkswagen AG 
Blume added: “We believe in open markets, but openness also means standing up for our own interests in Europe. Because a strong industrial base means more than economic success. It protects technological independence.” 
Volkswagen is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years. Blume emphasised the “close ties between France and Germany”, while hosting the French industry minister, Sébastian Martin. 
Arno Antlitz, VW’s chief financial officer, said the job cuts were necessary to “increase our economic power” by increasing profitability and allowing it to defend its “home turf”. 
The company is cutting the number of models it offers worldwide from 150 to 75 across brands including Audi and Škoda. It hopes the move will reduce complexity in its factories and for dealers, cutting the cost of each vehicle it makes. 
On Sunday, it revealed the production version of its ID Tiguan, an electric edition of its bestselling family SUV.
